lines.text: A ribbon of land between the Andes and the sea, from the driest desert on Earth to the glaciers of Patagonia. This is the story of Chile.
It begins about two hundred million years ago, as the ocean floor dived beneath South America and pushed up the Andes, the longest mountain range on any continent.
In the north, the Atacama Desert formed, so dry that some places go years without rain, and so clear that today the world's telescopes gather there.
Some fourteen and a half thousand years ago, people were already living at Monte Verde in the south, among the oldest settlements in the Americas.
On the desert coast, Chinchorro fishing people began to mummify their dead, two thousand years before Egypt did.
In the south lived the Mapuche, a people who would hold off first the Incas and then the Spanish for centuries.
Far out in the Pacific, on the island that is now Chile's Easter Island, the Rapa Nui carved nearly a thousand giant stone figures, the moai.
In 1520 Ferdinand Magellan found a passage through the tip of the continent, the strait that still bears his name.
In 1541 the conquistador Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago, the city that would become Chile's capital.
Bernardo O'Higgins would fight beside San Martin for freedom from Spain, and lead the new country before dying in exile in Peru.
From 1810 Chileans fought for independence, and won it in the battles of Chacabuco and Maipu.
In 1818 Chile declared itself free, a long narrow nation between the mountains and the Pacific.
In the War of the Pacific, Chile took the nitrate deserts of the north from Peru and Bolivia, and with them great wealth.
Gabriela Mistral, a poet and teacher, would become the first Latin American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Pablo Neruda wrote love poems known around the world and the epic Canto General, and won the Nobel Prize too.
Salvador Allende, a doctor and socialist, would be elected president in 1970, and nationalise the country's key industries.
In the desert, the vast copper mine of Chuquicamata opened, one of the largest open pits on Earth.
Augusto Pinochet, born the same year, became the general who would overthrow Allende and rule with free markets and terrible abuses.
Michelle Bachelet, whose family suffered under the dictatorship, would become Chile's first woman president.
In Patagonia, the granite towers and glaciers of Torres del Paine became a national park.
In 1960 the strongest earthquake ever measured struck southern Chile, sending tsunamis across the Pacific as far as Hawaii and Japan.
Just two years later, Chile hosted the World Cup, and Brazil, led by Garrincha, won it again.
Jose Antonio Kast, born in 1966, would lead the conservatives and win the presidency in late 2025.
On the eleventh of September 1973 the military seized power. Allende died, and thousands of Chileans were killed or disappeared.
Gabriel Boric, a future student leader, would become president in 2022.
In 1988 Chileans were asked whether Pinochet should stay. They said no, and two years later democracy returned.
In 2010 another great earthquake shook Chile, one of the strongest ever recorded.
That same year, the world watched as thirty-three miners were brought up alive after sixty-nine days underground.
In 2019 huge protests against inequality filled the streets, and led Chileans to vote on writing a new constitution.
Shaken by earthquakes and dictatorship alike, Chile keeps rebuilding along its long thin strip of land.
